title: NPS — Basaltic Lava Flows
text: Most lava flows, including the ones from Kīlauea and Mauna Loa volcanoes in Hawai’i Volcanoes National Park, have basaltic compositions. The low silica concentrations in these lavas mean that they are highly fluid (e.g., have low viscosity) and they flow easily, forming lava flows that may travel great distances from the vent where they were erupted to cover broad areas of land. Basaltic lava flows may be erupted from shield volcanoes such as in Hawai’i, from vents at the base of a cinder cone such as Sunset Crater Volcano National Monument in Arizona, fissure volcanoes such as at Craters of the Moon National Monument in Idaho, and in monogenetic volcanic fields like at El Malpais National Monument in New Mexico. Basaltic lava flows usually either have pahoehoe or ‘a‘ā morphological forms. The surfaces of pahoehoe lava flows are smooth, ropy, or billowy, and ‘a‘ā flows are rough and clinkery.
